Title: The Asian Institute of Management's Annual Conference
text: The Asian Institute of Management s Annual Conference Makati, Philippines Plenary Session I: The Emerging Corporate Governance Structure in Asia: Western Model or Eastern Pragmatism? Speech by M.R. Pridiyathorn Devakula Governor, Bank of Thailand 4 September 2003 Ladies and Gentlemen: I am honoured to be here today and much appreciate an opportunity to address this prestigious gathering on the subject that I am most interested that of corporate governance. In my view, the way that Western culture built in the practice of good corporate governance has the potential to create problems and damages to businesses. Therefore, I think that it is crucial to build a correct understanding of the subject to safeguard our businesses from taking the wrong path. The past decade has seen a lot of discussions on the issue of good governance. Why? Did good governance not exist prior to this? Good governance is not a new invention. It is a principle by which good managers observe in the management of any organization. A good manager is naturally committed to the pursuit of efficiency, profitability, progress and advancement, safe and sustainable growth. This requires not only skills, but also integrity. Such moral values as honesty, integrity, diligence, accountability, and fairness, are values that are within the heart and mind of all good managers. Since the past decade, the topic of governance has become the talk of the town. Before that, businesses experienced phenomenal growth, and with intense competition, the emphasis was placed on volume or growth. Quality and integrity was cast aside. Eventually, this type of growth could not be sustained and the bubble burst. Then everybody started to think that they had taken the wrong path and turned around in search of management practice that will not bring down the organization one which would emphasize both quality and volume growth. Thus, the talk on corporate governance began. This realization led to the setting up of risk management committees to monitor and oversee the risk management function of the enterprise. This is a task that has always been part of traditional managerial responsibilities that is to ensure that the organization grows without undertaking unwarranted risks. Nevertheless, as the bubble burst, such a task was no longer entrusted solely to management, and risk management committees came into being. In addition, audit committees were also formed to identify potential problems and weaknesses in the organization, including those of management. Again, this is a responsibility that belonged directly to top management. However, because management was focusing solely on growth, causing damages to the organization, such a trust was no longer placed on them and an audit committee had to be formed. Another new addition to the governance package is the independent directors. The tasks of these directors are to ensure that management does not abuse its power and take advantage of the organization. Independent directors also oversee that the directors or management who represent the interests of large shareholders do not act against the interests of minority shareholders. Actually all these new governance elements would be unnecessary if only management would uphold the moral standard, and focus on quality and soundness instead of volume and high growth alone. These committees and independent directors would not be needed if only management put the collective interests of the organization, shareholders and employees first and foremost, instead of their own personal interests. In the Oriental world of the past, management s performance was measured by the soundness of the businesses one that continued to grow with stability and not be open to risks or failure. Good management was also measured by the contentment, pride and job satisfaction of its employees. The organization, in turn, would be recognized for its credibility. Management who could achieve all these would be honoured by society for his credibility. Thus, management had to be cautious and prudent in doing their job. They would ensure that there were neither unwarranted risks nor vulnerabilities. They would treat their employees like family members who would be with them for a long time, ensure that shareholders receive a stable return through regular dividend payouts, focus on long-term rather than short-term profits, ensure a gradual increase in stock price, and carefully guard the good name and reputation of the organization. In the last ten to twenty years, the Oriental world started to absorb Western influences. Success came to be measured by the size of the firm, profit, asset value, and personal net worth and management income. Society came to honour the wealthy rather than the good managers. Management was lured by offers of profit sharing and stock options. As a result, modern management focused on high growth and short-term profits, and risk taking for the sake of higher growth and bigger profits. The aim was to drum up the public s perception that the business had growth potential in order to push up stock price, which would then benefit the stock option. Those who were smart knew how to dress up their balance sheet to enhance growth, and at times, greed would also tempt them to do just that. We already saw this happen during the Enron and Worldcom episodes. Between profit sharing and stock options, profit sharing is less dangerous because it comes from real operating results. Stock options, however, are given based on expected performance, which is easier to paint. In some Western organizations, the structure of monetary incentive for management is not well balanced. Income from profit incentive is greater than half of total income, and basic salary is lower than half of income. This clearly is a recipe for danger and temptation to be lured by short-term gains at the expense of the long term interest of the organization. The worst though, is that some organizations offer stock options not only to management but also to the Board of Directors who are supposed to oversee management s performance. In this case, the Board too will be subjected to the same temptation. Thus when management presents the balance sheet or projects that stand to make short-term profits and send stock price soaring, to which the Board stands to gain, they may stop asking questions which they should be asking, even though they may not be confident in the facts and the risks. Thus, even with the presence of independent directors, as in the case for both Worldcom and Enron, when the Board of Directors was tempted by the same desire and greed as those of management, their performance too was impaired. In short, Western culture plays on greed or desire. This results in management behaviour that is focused on quantity and not quality. This eventually leads to problems, which in turn gives rise to the need for corporate governance as a way to control quality. Then when the Board of Directors, who are supposed to be the guardian of this quality control process, are also tempted by this same desire, the control mechanism then breaks down. I think that the most important ingredient for corporate governance is the good conscience of management. If management does not possess a good conscience, and if the Board of Directors does not perform their role in balancing the power of management, then no such committees, be they risk management or audit committees or even independent directors, will ever resolve this problem. One additional issue needs to be explored that is the Chairmanship of the CEO. Yes, the Board of Directors has a duty to balance the power of management. However, in practice, there are a lot of American companies where the Chairman of the Board is the same person as the CEO, which is a model that promotes effective leadership. At the same time, this model undermines the control function of the Board of Directors. The CEO then assumes the responsibility of the Chairman in setting the agenda for the Board meeting as well as the direction or the tone of the meeting. Thus a Chairman who is also a CEO will be able to abuse this power and set the meeting agenda to present only the issues he wants other Board members to know, leaving out the other issues that he wants to hide. I am not implying that having risk management or audit committees or independent directors is not a good idea. These governance elements are certainly useful and I do not doubt it for a minute. But they became necessary when incipient Western influences and materialism, together with tempting offers linked to profits and volume growth, influenced the good conscience of management. These governance elements were thus needed to provide a check and balance of the power of management at all times. I want to re-emphasize that if we start on the right path with a management team that has a good conscience, we will not have to be burdened by these unnecessary monitoring and controls. But if we begin with tempting offers, which go against quality and moral, we will have to deal with these issues endlessly. In reality, we must accept that we live in a material world where business success is still measured by volume growth, thus control mechanism in forms of committees become increasingly important. The most effective preventative way to promote enterprises growth, continued profits and integrity, is to choose the management with a good conscience. Of course, management with skills in promoting volume growth is necessary to ensure business success. But management with a good conscience is the key to a long-lived success. Furthermore, the use of profits and growth as a measure of success of the firm creates temptation for management. This should be reviewed seriously. Is it really necessary? If it is so, it is crucial to set requirement that cannot be easily abused together with clear monitoring guidelines. Moreover, performance incentives in the form of profit sharing or stock options should be reasonable, not excessive. It should also be structured in a way that is well balanced compared to the basic compensation as already mentioned earlier. In addition, to ensure that the management power is effectively controlled, the Chairman of the Board should not be the same person as the CEO. Compensation system for the Board of Directors should be different from that of management. This is because while management has a tendency to focus on growth and short-term profits, the Board of Directors should take a longer term perspective and ensure the soundness of the business. Thus, compensation of the Board of Directors should not be linked to short-term gains such as profit sharing and stock options. A provision of respectable director fees and due social recognition, would make them perform their duty of supervision and oversight more effectively, thus ensuring the enterprise s sustainability in the long-run. Most importantly, directors and especially the Chairman should be persons well-known for long record of good conduct and well-known for their integrity so they would not risk their reputation for some short term gain. Talent and smartness are necessary ingredients for a directorship; but integrity and ethics are much more important. Thank you.

Title: The Role of Non-Bank Financial Institutions in relation to Monetary Policy
text: The Role of Non-Bank Financial Institutions in relation to Monetary Policy By Mr. Thirachai Phuvanat naranubala Deputy Governor, Bank of Thailand At Regional Seminar on Non-Bank Financial Institutions in East Asia Region Bangkok September 4, 2002 I wish to congratulate the Securities and Exchange Commission of Thailand and The World Bank for organizing such an interesting seminar in Bangkok, and to thank them for inviting me to share my thoughts with you today. I can see that the topics in the seminar will cover many important aspects of non-bank financial institutions' operations -- ranging from the regulatory and supervisory framework to capital market development as well as the issue of governance. But I am the only person touching on monetary policy aspect. Monetary policy does affect an important part of your business, which is the bond market. Because the one factor reflected in the bond market yield curve is inflation expectation. Therefore, if the framework and the conduct of monetary policy result in low and predictable inflation, it will help curb volatility of the yield curve and support development of the bond markets. Change in monetary policy stance also directly affect interest rate and hence the bond market. Thus, it pays for you to understand monetary policy. Monetary Policy in Thailand In order for you to do that, I have to start by telling you about how the monetary policy framework has evolved here in Thailand. Since the end of the Second World War, Thailand employed the regime of fixed exchange rate one way or another. At the beginning our currency was fixed to the British Pound, and later to the US Dollar -- first directly, then later via a basket with a very heavy US Dollar content. The regime had served us very well. It provided certainty for international trade, and it helped to attract foreign investment. We were able to maintain the parity with the US Dollar for more than 18 years until 1981 when we had our first devaluation. The pressure on our parity in the early days was slight. Thailand's exports at that time were rice, rubber, tin and teak. Our production costs for those items were among the lowest in the world. However, beginning from the 1980's, we began to industrialize. Our industrial exports which was only 33 % of the total exports at the end of the 1970's quickly rose to 76 % in 1990 and even further to 86% today. With industrialization, we began to find that our productivity did not keep up with our major trading partners, particularly the US, and pressure on the parity began to build up. Our domestic costs of production have never been flexible downward. To ask for a wage and salary reduction was unthinkable then - as it is today. Our only choice was to devalue. The devaluations that occurred were not always smooth. More than once, they brought on political tension, between those in the government who believed in it and those in the opposition, or even the military, who thought otherwise. In one incident, it even caused a change in the central bank governor. Finally, we had to float our currency in 1997. Since then, we have adopted Inflation Targeting as our monetary policy framework. A core inflation target was announced at between 0 and 3.5 % per annum. The central bank will regularly monitor economic changes and make forecasts. If we see that the rate of inflation has a tendency to exceed the range, we will adopt a tighter monetary policy stance by increasing the policy interest rate, and vice versa if we see it going under the range. The policy rate that we use is the 14 day repurchase rate. This is completely different, of course, compared to the days of fixed currency regime when interest rates in Thailand would move mostly in tandem with the US rates. The change in the monetary policy framework therefore affects the financial environment and your businesses a great deal. Development of the bond market What other change also happened? One very important change that has occurred in Thailand is the rapid development of the bond market, which took off after the 1997 crisis. The bond market is an important tool for safety and soundness of the financial institution system. It allows the intermediation process to proceed uninterrupted when the banks are temporarily in difficulty. But more importantly, it helps with liquidity management. In the case of Thailand, the government throughout the 1980's had been very disciplined in their fiscal policy. They maintained balanced budgets in most years. As a result, no new government bond was issued, as old ones were being retired. Without a deep and liquid government bond market, growth of corporate bond was also slow. When the crisis erupted, financial institutions that could not seek liquidity from the inter bank market were stuck without liquid instruments in hand. Some of them might have survived had the bond market been more active. After the crisis, the government had to issue massive amount of bonds to cover losses in the financial system. Today, the Thai bond market is therefore much larger, at 38 % of the GDP. We have a much more active market. What does an active bond market mean to monetary policy? I will highlight three points. First is the implication on transmission mechanism. When the central bank wants to change stance in monetary policy, it changes interest rate up or down. But it does not directly change the interest rates along the whole spectrum of the yield curve. It only affects the key policy rate, which in the case of Thailand is the very short-term 14 day rate in the repurchase market. However, to have an impact on the real economy, there must be a way to transmit this signal all the way to the financial activities that determine economic transactions, such as business capital formation, household consumption and savings. The traditional channel is through commercial banks. And now we have another channel through the corporate bond market. This channel is poised to grow more rapidly in the future. The second aspect is that central bank also operates in the government bond market in its conduct of monetary policy. It can sell and buy bonds to pump money in or out of the system, through their open market operations. An efficient, deep and liquid bond market therefore will not only help make the intermediation process competitive and active - but also allow the central bank to transact in the market more effectively. The third aspect is the function of the bond market in managing the capital flows. Emerging market economies when they are successful tend to attract capital inflow very quickly, and in very large quantity. Unfortunately, if things turn bad, the outflow of capital can also be equally quick and in as large a quantity. How can one better manage this volatile capital flow? To some extent, I think the risks can be mitigated with a well functioning bond market. If we can make it to function as a temporary reservoir to store the incoming water, and more slowly releasing it to the various users of fund within the country, at the right pace for absorption -- if the market selection process can be made such that only the projects with really viable, economic prospects are granted the fund - and, if the foreign owners of fund can be persuaded to hold the instruments denominated in borrowers' own currency, thereby shifting the position on the foreign exchange risks from the borrowers to the investors, then the bond market can be a safer channel for capital flows than the commercial banks. At this point you may disagree that if foreign investors in bonds want out, they will still sell the bonds, causing the prices to be sharply lower anyway. This is true. But price volatility in the bond market is still better than a run on your banks. Therefore an efficient bond market can help lessen the adverse impact that volatile capital flows may have on the financial institutions. A sound financial system is of course a necessary condition for the conduct of monetary policy. The role of non-bank financial institutions Let me now turn to the non-bank financial institutions. What can be your roles in relation to monetary policy? I can offer four suggestions. Number one, you can make yourself an efficient player in the market. The more efficient the competitors, the better the market is. But in order to compete well, you will have to be well capitalized, well organized with good governance and risk management processes. Number two, you can help establish market codes and practices that conform to world standards. The market needs rules to ensure smooth trades and dispute resolutions, and to guard against manipulation. The industry has an important role to play in the setting of rules and codes of conduct. Number three, you can help ensure that the market has a wide variety of products. We should aim for a market that can offer many kinds of contract, to serve those needing to unbundled or rearrange all kinds of risks at competitive prices. And lastly, you can build for yourselves a good analytical capability. It will prevent herd behavior, and help to stabilize the market. But more importantly, proper project analysis can ensure that capital is channeled only to the good projects. It can help prevent over expansion of businesses, over diversification and over enthusiasm that inevitably winds up as non-performing loans in the end. Ladies and gentlemen The task of the central bank in monetary policy is to ensure that it sets the right policy, and that its policy is transmitted through to the overall economy. The financial system through which their policy is transmitted must also be safe and sound. Non-bank financial institutions do indeed have vital roles to play here. ---------------------------------------------

Title: Supervisory Concerns in an IT Environment at SEACEN/ Federal Reserve System Courseon Electronic Banking and Technology Risk Supervision Bangkok, Thailand
text: Supervisory Concerns in an IT Environment by Dr. Tarisa Watanagase Deputy Governor, Bank of Thailand at SEACEN/ Federal Reserve System Course on Electronic Banking and Technology Risk Supervision Bangkok, Thailand 4 September 2003 ________________________ As IT is becoming a major driver in banking industry nowadays, supervisors will have to be prepared and keep up with the developments. Today is a good opportunity for me to share some of our thoughts and experiences with you in this area. This presentation will cover 1. Market Development 2. Supervisory Concerns 3. Supervisory Challenges 4. BoT's Regulations on issues related to E-Banking 5. Future Trend 1. Market Development For decades, financial institutions used technology almost exclusively for their back office processing. Now, technology has moved out front to almost all aspects of their services. Technology is a key aspect of many business decisions and many new products rely on new technologies. Technological innovation and competition among financial institutions and nonfinancial institutions have called for a much wider array of financial products and services to become accessible and to be delivered to retail and wholesale customers through electronic distribution channels, referred to as electronic banking. In Thailand, e-banking has been around for some time, financial institutions have been using technology to provide electronic capabilities in the form of automated teller machines and telephone banking. More recently, e-banking has been transformed by the internet. It is a new delivery channel for banking services that benefit both customers and banks. Banks can provide services more efficiently and at lower costs. It also allows banks to penetrate new markets and thus expand their geographical reach and helps improve efficiency and quality of financial services as well as feebased income business. For customers, e-banking makes it easier to compare banks' services and products, thus increasing competition among banks. Electronic banking services offered by the majority of banks include phone banking, automated teller machines, electronic fund transfer, Internet banking, and mobile banking. Although the benefits of these electronic services are quite clear, consumers, both retail and corporate, are still reluctant to utilize the services. A survey conducted late last year here in Thailand reveals that consumers still prefer to conduct banking transaction in the traditional manner, i.e. having face to face contact with human tellers. Consumers' perception regarding e-banking is still not very positive. The main reasons of not using the electronic services are that consumers are not sure about the accuracy of the services and that some electronic services do not provide transaction evidence, which consumers think they still need should problems or disputes arise. For retail consumers, lack of knowledge to use the electronic services is also a reason why they tend to transact at banks' branches instead of electronic terminals. While retail consumers are familiar with the use of automated teller machines, only a small fraction of them transact via phone or Internet. According to the survey, high-income retail consumers tend to utilize phone banking and Internet banking more often than do low income consumers. Usage of phone banking and Internet banking by corporate customers is still low, though large and medium corporates tend to use phone banking and Internet banking more often than do small corporates. 2. Supervisory Concerns Innovation associated with IT and e-banking also brings in new risks and new dimension to the traditional risk of financial and payment systems, thus requiring careful considerations by regulators in supervising the IT and e-banking activities. 2.1 Risks associated with IT and E-Banking 1. Operational risk Operational risk is the risk arising from the delivery of services or products. This type of risk often results from failure to establish adequate security measures, contingency plans, testing, and auditing standards. Operational risk can increase when a financial institution hires outside service providers to design products, services, delivery channels, and processes that do not fit with the financial institution's systems or customer demands. Deficiencies in system design, implementation, or maintenance of systems or equipment also increase this type of risk. Thus, the regulators have to ensure that financial institutions have adequate security measures, contingency plans, and auditing standards in place. 2. Reputational Risk Reputation risk is the risk arising from negative public opinion. Reputation risk arises whenever technology-based banking products, services, delivery channels, or processes may generate adverse public opinion. For example, breaches of security and disruptions to the system's availability can damage financial institutions' reputation. Also, system disruptions or doubts about the integrity of the system or data could result in a loss of confidence in electronic delivery channels as a whole, and can potentially affect other e-banking providers. Therefore, regulators need to provide guidelines for risk management and also encourage financial institutions to educate their customers of safety procedures in obtaining e-banking services. 3. Compliance risk Compliance risk is the risk arising from violations of, or non-conformance with, laws, rules, regulations, or ethical standards. Some new technologies raise unexpected compliance issues. For example, transactions conducted through the internet can also raise questions regarding jurisdictional authority over those transactions. Cross border activities raise a number of concerns to supervisors on how to supervise banking businesses with no physical presence in the country, and also how to effectively manage risks involved in cross-border transactions. In this regard, Basel Committee on Banking Supervision has suggested that in order to supervise cross border e-banking activities, effective home country supervision has to be in place, as well as continued international cooperation between banking supervisors. 4. Strategic Risk Strategic risk is the risk arising from adverse business decisions or improper implementation of those decisions. Use of technology can create strategic risk when management does not adequately plan for, manage, and monitor the performance of technology-related products, services, processes, and delivery channels. On this matter, regulators have to ensure that financial institutions have carefully considered its strategic risk, and are prepared for its future development of core businesses. 2.2 Risk Management Framework Key to the technology-related risk management process is to identify, measure, monitor, and control risk exposure. Basically, the process involves three essential elements. 1) Plan for the use of technology. Three basic components of an effective planning process are: - Involving Senior Management and Board of Directors in Decision-making. The board of directors and senior management should review, approve, and monitor technology projects that may have a significant impact on the financial institution's operations, earnings or capital. Also, the board should be fully informed by senior management, on an ongoing basis, of the risks that technology projects may pose to the bank. - Gathering and Analyzing Information. Financial institutions should gather and analyze relevant information regarding new and existing technologies and evaluate how new technologies will fit into existing systems. Management should assess current and developing industry standards in determining whether to implement specific technologies. - Assessing Needs and Reviewing Options. Management should carefully assess the costs and benefits of adopting new technology, and consider whether the necessary resources, time, and expertise are available to complete any new technology proposal successfully. Risks, financial consequences, and likelihood that certain risks may occur should also be evaluated. 2) Decide how to implement the technology Proper project implementation includes controls, policies and procedures, training, testing, contingency planning, and proper oversight of any outsourcing. Specifically, financial institutions should establish necessary controls to avoid operational failures and unauthorized intrusions, which could result in losses and damaged reputation. Management should also ensure proper coordination and integration of projects among managers, work units, and team members. 3) Measure and Monitor Performance Management should monitor and measure the performance of technology-related products, services, delivery channels, and processes to benchmark against its intended results. Financial institutions should establish clearly defined measurement objectives and conduct periodic reviews to ensure that goals and standards established by the management are met. 2.3 IT Security One of the most important assets of an organization is information. Consequently, security controls are needed to safeguard information from unauthorized modification, destruction, and disclosure. The degree of controls should be based on an assessment of risks in relation to the value and the sensitivity of the information. As financial institutions increasingly utilize technology infrastructure to offer products and services to their customers, security controls must never be underestimated. General risks which could affect the security of the e-banking services include false authentication of parties to a transaction, interception of information being transmitted, and unauthorized access to information or systems. Regulators must ensure that financial institutions have appropriate practices in place to guarantee the confidentiality of data, as well as the integrity of the system and data. It is also important for regulators to ensure that financial institutions are prepared for the interruption in their systems and are able to recover the systems as needed. Security Controls Management should ensure that appropriate security processes are in place for e-banking. Security controls should aim to address these issues: 1) Access control Financial institutions should establish sufficient access controls, both physical and logical, in order to prevent unauthorized access to applications and databases. Adequate security infrastructure should be deployed to maintain appropriate boundaries and restrictions on both internal and external user activities. 2) Authentication Financial institutions should use reliable methods to properly authenticate and authorize customers seeking to initiate electronic transactions. Failure to adequately authenticate customers could result in unauthorized access to e-banking accounts, financial loss, and reputational damage. 3) Data confidentiality Financial institutions should take appropriate measures to preserve confidentiality of key e-banking information. The measures should be commensurate with the sensitivity of the information being either transmitted over the networks or stored in databases. 4) System & Data integrity Financial institutions should ensure that appropriate measures are in place to ascertain the accuracy, completeness and reliability of e-banking transactions, records and information that is either transmitted over the networks or stored in databases. 5) System availability Effective capacity and business continuity planning processes are required to maintain public confidence. Key considerations associated with maintaining high system availability are effective contingency plans, adequate system capacity, reliable performance, fast response time, and swift recovery capability. 6) System detection Financial institutions should monitor their networks and systems on an ongoing basis to detect any unusual transactions, unusual activities, and suspected intrusions. Management needs to stay abreast of new threats and vulnerabilities and keeps up to date on latest security patches or version upgrades in order to fix security flaws in the networks and systems. 7) Incident response Financial institutions should develop appropriate incident response plans to manage, contain and minimize problems arising from unexpected events, including internal and external attacks that may hamper the provision of e-banking services. 3. Supervisory Challenges While the financial industry is moving fast with innovations and developments, the primary objective for supervisors is still to ensure the stability of the financial system. Supervisors need to encourage financial institutions to operate their businesses in a safe and sound manner as new delivery channels, such as the internet, could exacerbate some of the same risks inherent in traditional banking. However, the prudential regulatory framework has to be congruent to the evolution of the e-banking business. Therefore we need to strike a balance between the need to maintain the stability of the financial system and to foster developments, competition, and a level playing field. To foster innovation: There is a need for regulators to keep up with the development of the market while being proactive in formulating the regulatory framework. In the case of Thailand, BOT takes an active role in meeting regularly with financial institutions to exchange views and experiences on the development of the businesses and IT environment. In the process of drafting policies, we often seek out the view of our fellow regulators to ensure that our policy are in line with market and international practices, as well as to help us anticipate problems that may arise in implementation. The final drafts of policies are sent out for comments from key stakeholders in and outside the Bank of Thailand, especially the industry, to ensure that the policies are practical and not posing any undue burden on financial institutions. We also make sure that revision of regulations and guidelines is conducted regularly to ensure that e-banking policies are keeping with demand from the financial community as well as with market innovation and international best practices. To ensure the stability of financial system We have adopted risk-based method in our banking supervision where examiners assess types and levels of risk associated with e-banking activities and comment on significant deficiencies and recommend corrective actions and ways to mitigate risks of the financial institutions. Risk assessment is conducted both quantitatively and qualitatively. The quantitative assessment includes size, complexity, and volume of the products and services. The more customers, services, and complexity of the services, the more risk. While the qualitative assessment focuses on risk management policy and capabilities, internal and security controls, monitoring and auditing process, and outsourcing policy. In addition, examiners also determine if the financial institutions are complying with all applicable laws, rules, and regulations. 4. BoT's Regulations on issues related to E-Banking Issued Regulations Currently, the Bank of Thailand is in the process of formulating policy framework on ebanking issues with an aim to encourage financial institutions in Thailand to conduct e-banking business in a safe and sound manner as well as to protect consumer rights. It is also to ensure that the supervision framework is keeping up with demand from the financial community as well as with market innovation, international best practices and consistent with Thailand's Electronic Transaction Bill, which has been effective since April 2002. In recent years, BOT has issued supervisory guidelines and regulations relating to ebanking activities such as security requirements on ATM services, guidelines and criteria pertaining to Electronic Funds Transfer (EFT), and recently has issued a notification on requirements for the usage of internet network to support banking services, and IT outsourcing guidelines. 1. Usage of internet network to support banking services Financial institutions need to seek approval from the BOT prior to the use of the internet to conduct banking business. In order to get approval, the financial institutions have to prove that they have adequate security measures, risk management policy, internal control, contingency plan, and staff development plan. In addition to providing the banking services, commercial banks can display logos of other businesses on their web sites so that their customers know they can make payments to those businesses. However, underlying transactions with those businesses cannot be made on the banks' web sites. To date, the BOT has granted approval to nineteen financial institutions to undertake banking business via the internet. Example of internet banking services are: account inquiry, fund transfer, bills payment, financial market information, statement issuance, cheque cancellation, and ID & password change, and for wholesale services including cash management, FX trading, trade financing, loan services, and L/C services. 2. IT outsourcing By the advent of rapid change in technology and competition amongst financial institutions, financial institutions tend to reduce costs and to improve their services by outsourcing some technology-related functions such as data processing and system development to third parties both within and across borders. Such outsourcing can result in both benefits and risks to both financial institutions and their clients. Benefits such as an increase in domestic and international competitiveness of financial institutions may come at the risk of information leakage or sometimes of being dependent on inexperienced and below standard providers. As such, the Bank of Thailand has developed a guideline for IT outsourcing, which was circulated for comments from the industry, and announced in second quarter of 2003. The guideline requires financial institutions to develop IT policies that clearly state the reason and objective for IT outsourcing, risk management procedures, service provider selection procedures, the key features of the contract signed between financial institutions and the IT service provider, the monitoring and performance evaluation of the IT service provider, as well as consistency between related parties' IT contingency plans. The key point emphasized is that IT out-sourcing does not absolve the financial institution from its obligation to ensure safe and efficient services to clients, and to comply with the regulatory framework, as if it had not outsourced the services. To foster accountability, both the financial institution's IT policies and risk management procedures must be deliberated and approved by the financial institution's Board of Directors. Work in the pipeline Apart from the issued rules and regulations, BOT is currently in the process of issuing further guidelines concerning the best practices in IT operations, such as IT insourcing, EBanking security, and Business Continuity Plan, and IT governance. 3. IT Insourcing While financial institutions are allowed to outsource their IT functions to service providers to reduce cost and improve efficiency of their services, currently they are not allowed to provide the same services to other companies. Bank of Thailand, however, sees the potential of financial institutions in technology developments. We believe that financial institutions' expertise in banking business coupled with their technology skill can foster developments in banking services. Thus, to promote a level playing field in the system and the development of modern business operations, and to allow financial institutions to optimize their IT resources, the BOT is developing a framework to permit commercial banks to provide IT services to other financial institutions. The regulation will require financial institutions to have in place their Board's approved policy on the matter which must contain the objective, risk management procedures, contingency plans, and internal control procedures. However, in providing IT services to other companies, financial institutions must ensure appropriate scope and avoid straying too far outside its core banking business. They have to bear in mind that the insourcing is meant to optimize existing assets and avoid idle resources. 4. E-banking security Financial institutions that offer transactional E-Banking services will be subject to security threats from a wide range of sources. There is a need to strengthen the management of IT security in general and their transactional E-Banking services in particular. Thus, the BOT has drafted a policy statement governing E-banking security and has already sent out the draft to the industry for comments. The key features of the guideline covers provision for services that customers can directly initiate a transaction, such as internet banking services, which are carried over open networks and subject to operational risks and computer crimes. Therefore, these can significantly affect the financial institution and the system-wide reputational risk and client's confidence. The guideline requires the financial institution to carefully consider business strategy for providing e-banking business, and draw up a Board's approved plan that addresses a comprehensive set of issues, which cover risk scenario and assessment, risk management procedure, and suggestions on how to improve the environment to enhance security. The risk management procedures should cover key process/issues such as: access control; authentication and non-repudiation, system and data integrity; data confidentiality; system availability and contingency plan; system detection of intrusion and vulnerabilities such as audit log; and procedures for incident response and reporting. The suggestions on how to improve the environment to enhance security include issues of outsourcing and internal control, employee education and training, and consumer education since consumer is usually a weak link in security chain that is susceptible to hacker. 5. IT business continuity plan (IT BCP) In 1998, the Bank of Thailand has issued a regulation to all commercial banks that if they use computer systems to support their operations and services, they must have contingency plans and maintain computer backup systems outside the buildings that house main computer systems. The downtime of banking services due to computer systems failure must not be longer than one working day. However, as we are exposed to a wide range of threats such as natural disaster, terrorist attacks, or computer viruses, which could disrupt financial operations, there is a need for financial institutions to be prepared for those disruptions and ensure their business continuity. The Bank of Thailand is now revising the regulation and focuses more on risk management principle and the FIs management Board's oversight and responsibility. The new policy guideline will require financial institutions to develop and implement an IT business continuity plan. The key issues to be included in the financial institution's IT business continuity plan are integrating IT business continuity plan into the overall risk management plan; requirements on data and system recovery; assignment of responsibility and accountability; and testing procedures of the plan. This is to ensure that when IT risks occur, the financial institution has a plan to make sure that all key businesses would function properly so as to reduce expected loss from this operational risk. The essence is that the plan generated by the institution, such as back-up facility and recovery, must be commensurate with the level of risk of the institution. 6. IT Governance During the last few years, financial institutions have increasingly invested in technology infrastructure to improve their internal processes and their servicing capabilities. Investment in technology infrastructure normally involves huge amount of funds and other resources. Technology also carries risks, which can adversely affect financial institutions if not properly managed. Financial institutions need to understand the strategic importance of IT, manage IT to effectively deliver value to business, and mitigate risks arising from the use of IT. The BOT is developing a guideline on IT governance, which will focus on how financial institutions make the best use of their invested technologies. The guideline will provide financial institutions with high-level IT control framework related to the formulation of IT strategies, the management of IT processes to deliver value, the performance measurement, and the management of IT-related risks. We believe that effective IT governance process will enable financial institutions to effectively utilized their technologies to meet business' expectations and to add value to their business. In that way, IT will truly help the organizations to improve competitive advantage, customer satisfaction, cost efficiency, and ability to grow and innovate the business. Eventually, it will help financial institutions to realize better return on investment in technology infrastructure. 5. Future Trend To date, most banks have combined the new electronic delivery channels with traditional banking services. The use of IT will be the major driver of banking services development, as it provides enormous benefits to both consumers and banks. The benefits are in terms of ease and cost of transactions of consumers, increased banks productivity in providing services, and new business opportunities. With the rapid development in technology, in the near future, apart from the known internet banking, we will see more of the "non-traditional" banking products. The examples of the initiatives that are being launched in the market are e-money in the form of stored value cards, and prepaid cards in foreign currency for customers to cash out their money abroad. The providers of these services will not only be limited to banks, but also non-banks. Of course, the extent to which a non-bank provider can offer these new services and products depends on the rules and regulations of each country. Striking a proper balance between service providers that are banks and non-banks will be a challenge for the authorities. Lastly, as mentioned, the cross border activities will be inevitable. In this open and changing environment, supervisors need to be proactive and clearly state their direction in supervising such activities. It is also their job to educate the public of the safe and sound manner in adopting the services. We need to carefully consider the risks inherent in adopting these services and products, as well as to protect the consumers. Coordination of banking supervisors at the international level is also needed. As for banks, they need to maintain a secure and reliable systems that would attract more customers while retaining existing customers. They also need to encourage their customers to utilize the readily available electronic banking services, as well as to educate their customers on how to use the services in a safety manner. As long as the technology is changing and financial institutions are still depending on it, not only that financial institutions need to be careful in adopting the right technology for their needs and be aware of the risks involved in adopting those technology, but we, as the regulators, need to be sure that we are keeping up with the changing environment and are on top of the issues.

Title: Thailand : Recent Economic Performance and the Road Ahead at the British Chamber of Commerce Thailand Luncheon, The Conrad Bangkok
text: Thailand: Recent Economic Performance and the Road Ahead (Revisited) by M.R. Pridiyathorn Devakula Governor of the Bank of Thailand at the British Chamber of Commerce Thailand luncheon The Conrad Bangkok 5 September 2005 1 Honourable guests, ladies and gentlemen, It has been almost two years since I was last invited by the British Chamber of Commerce Thailand to speak about the economy, and I thank you all for inviting me to speak again today. I have chosen to address the old issue of Thailands economic performance and the road ahead so to update you on how the Bank of Thailand views the current economic performance and what we see as the challenges that lie ahead. Compared to the past couple of years when the Thai economy enjoyed strong growth accompanied by low inflation and current account surpluses, the situation now looks considerably less favourable. Let me give you some comparisons. GDP growth of 6.1% last year dipped by half to only 3.3% in the first quarter of this year before bouncing to 4.4% in the second quarter. Meanwhile, the current account went from a strong surplus of 7.1 billion US dollars last year to a sizeable deficit of 6.2 billion US dollars during the first half of this year. The reversal was abrupt and of significant magnitude, and two key questions are: What happened to the Thai economy? and Will such deterioration continue? My answer to the first question of What happened to the Thai economy? is that we were struck by a perfect storm. Many adverse shocks hit the economy simultaneously between the latter half of 2004 and early 2005. The dominant one is, of course, the high world oil prices, but also influential are the prolonged drought, the tsunami and unrest in the Southern part of Thailand, and the downturn of the global electronics cycle and the slowdown in global demand that have dampened our exports. Lets look at each of them in turn. 2 Five years ago, a barrel of Dubai crude oil cost round 23 US dollars, and today it has nearly reached 60 US dollars. The doubling of crude oil prices undoubtedly has a negative impact on an oil-importing country like Thailand, but especially so when the country is highly dependent on oil. Compared to other countries, even China, Thailand scores poorly in terms of oil efficiency. For every unit of GDP produced, we use more oil than most countries. When we tabulate the contribution of key factors to the deterioration in the current account, it is evident that oil has been dominant, accounting for roughly half of the deterioration. Moreover, higher oil prices have translated into higher production costs and contributed to the slowdown in manufacturing production during the first half of 2005. Besides lowering growth and causing the current account to worsen, an important side effect of higher oil prices is inflation. The sharp acceleration in headline inflation from 2.7% this past January to 5.6% in August is mainly a result of higher oil prices. Ladies and gentlemen, The second shock that hit the economy is the drought. With it, crop production shrank by as much as 9.7% in the first quarter of this year before the situation eased up a bit in the second quarter. The saving grace is that crop prices have gone up as a result of diminished supply, so farm income has not been affected and continues to support the expansion of household consumption in rural areas. The third shock is the tsunami that stuck the Andaman coast late last year coupled with occasional eruptions of unrest in the three 3 Southern-most provinces. The combination has led to a sudden drop in the number of foreign visitors to the popular tourist destinations on the Andaman coast in the wake of the natural disaster and also to a slow recovery since. The fourth shock is the slowdown in exports demand that has been driven partly by the overall slower growth of major economies and aggravated by the electronics cycle, which hit a bottom in the first quarter of this year. Ladies and gentlemen, What has been intriguing, however, is the fact that the economy was hit by a perfect storm and yet the NPL ratio has not gone up. Bank profitability continues to be sound, and bank credits are expanding quite healthily, despite being affected somewhat by dampened business confidence during the past few months. On the whole, the banking sector is sound and supportive of economic growth. Turning to the corporate sector, we see profitability continuing to grow as well. Although the current account has been in deficits, international reserves have stayed above 48 billion US dollars throughout the past 9 months, and the ratio of reserves to short-term debt of over 3 times indicates that Thailand has no problem with external liquidity. As a result, the exchange rate has fluctuated within its normal range. Meanwhile, the public sector helps to support economic stability by maintaining fiscal prudence, as indicated by the ratio of public debt to GDP of well below 50% and falling. On the whole, what do these statistics say? I think they all point toward the resilience of the economy to withstand adverse shocks and 4 our inherent strength to charge forward once the turbulence subsides. Then, the next question is, When will the turbulence die down? Ladies and gentlemen, In my opinion, things should begin to clear up for the Thai economy in the second half of this year. First of all, it is very unlikely that we will be hit by another devastating disaster as the tsunami. Secondly, as mentioned earlier, the drought conditions have improved, even though there remains some uncertainty regarding water supply for the Eastern Seaboard industrial estate. Thirdly, exports are beginning to pick up. In July, exports grew by 16.8%, up from the average of 12.4% in the first half of this year. While it may be too soon to draw conclusion from the July exports figure alone, we have also seen a pickup in the production of export-oriented industries since the second quarter, especially electronics. This is an encouraging leading indicator, and the Bank of Thailand has forecasted that exports are likely to grow by (over) 16-17% in the second half of the year. Not only that the atmosphere should clear up, but there are also growth drivers in store. Along with exports, private investment is likely to step up and become a key driver of growth going forward. The demand for investment is driven to a large part by rising industrial capacity utilization. When the economy first emerged from the crisis a few years back, our capacity utilization rate was below 50%. Now the average for the entire industrial sector has risen to above 70%, with several key industries operating well above 80%, including petrochemicals, pulp and paper, commercial cars, and motorcycles. This means many businesses are soon to hit their production limit and thus new investment must take 5 place to relieve that constraint. As the corporate sector is seeing higher profits and rising retained earnings, it can easily opt to draw on own financial resources to undertake investment. Furthermore, unlike 2-3 years ago, banks are now willing to lend to the corporate sector, with loans to listed non-financial firms growing in the double-digit range. Therefore, financial conditions should not pose any constraints on firms. Besides private investment, public investment is likely to accelerate with the governments mega project plans. These mega projects are certainly beneficial to growth, both in the short-term when investment activities take place and in the longer-term when they help to alleviate logistic bottlenecks for the private sector. The only major caution is their side effect on the current account, and I will return to this point shortly. Another contributing factor to the recovery in GDP growth on the horizon is a mitigation of import growth. Although an acceleration in exports is usually accompanied by an acceleration of imports, especially imports of raw materials, things look different for Thailand in the second half of this year due to a couple of reasons. First and foremost, domestic oil consumption should begin to curtail in response to the floating of retail diesel prices last June. At the same time, recent energy conservation campaigns by the public sector have begun to bear fruit. In addition, the accumulation of steel, iron, and gold which took place in the first half of the year in anticipation of price increases suggests that the rest of this year should witness a slower growth rate of such import items. Given these likely developments, the Bank of Thailand anticipates an improvement in GDP growth during the latter half of 2005, and the entire years growth average of around 4% is reasonable. In 6 2006, growth will improve to over 5% as private investment steps up, mega project investment comes into play, and exports continue to recover. GDP growth is therefore not a concern in the view of the Bank of Thailand. What remains an issue is the current account. While we do expect to see the current account rebounding into surpluses for the second half of this year as a result of lower oil consumption, accelerating exports, and improving tourism, a total deficit of around 4 billion US dollars is nevertheless projected for the entire year. Moreover, the deficit is likely to stay on for the next few years due to three factors, namely, the acceleration in private investment, the speeding up of mega projects, and oil prices that are most likely to remain high. Ladies and gentlemen, The prospects of world oil prices falling substantially within the next 3-4 years are slim, given the lack of investment in oil production capacity over the past few years. In order to induce new exploration of oil supply, prices will have to stay sufficiently high for a sufficiently long period of time. But even if investment in new oil refineries begins today, it will take a couple of more years before they could start operation. Therefore, spare production capacity is likely to be low for quite some time. Meanwhile, world oil prices are expected to stay high and volatile and may occasionally shoot up in the event of threats to existing oil production facilities, such as geopolitical tensions or natural disasters. That brings me to the final part of my talkthe key policy implications going forward. As the present government is putting considerable attention on economic growth which is most likely to continue at a satisfactory pace, the Bank of Thailand would complement 7 by placing more emphasis on maintaining economic stability, for it is only when stability is achieved that growth can be sustained over the longer run. Given this, two challenges are on our agenda right now. First, we must keep inflation moderate; in particular, core inflation should not exceed 3.5% to preserve business and consumer confidence. In this regard, the Bank of Thailand has raised the policy interest rate six times over the past year to curb inflation. Second, external stability warrants continued attention. Although the countrys international reserves are at comfortable levels and help to uphold foreign investors confidence in the Thai economy, the prospect of persistent current account deficits implies the need for foreign saving to finance the countrys domestic resource gap. In order to attract quality capital inflowsand by that I mean foreign direct investment or long-term loansThailand will have to work on three aspects besides keeping inflation moderate as said before:  The exchange rate should not be too volatile, for high volatility tends to invite hot money that moves in and out swiftly for speculative purposes.  At the same time, domestic financial institutions must be sound in the eyes of foreign investors. In this respect, the Bank of Thailand has made significant progress. In the year 2000, Thai banks were incurring huge losses, but now they are generating profits, with the average return on assets at a healthy level of 1.6%. Meanwhile, the NPL burden has come down from 47% in 1998 to 10% currently, and the Bank of Thailand has a definite plan that would bring it down further. Furthermore, bank supervision has been beefed up, and the Bank of Thailand has 8 been resolute on the supervision standard as witnessed by the case of Krung Thai Bank. This last aspect has been particularly important in raising foreign investors confidence in Thai financial institutions as well as the economy as a whole.  The last issue that we need to work on is, of course, the current account itself. Most importantly, the deficits should be kept at manageable levels, preferably within 2-3% of GDP, and there are three important measures that would help. The first one is serious efforts by all parties to conserve energy. It is imperative to realize that the economys high degree of oil dependence today is a result of the lack of oil conservation efforts over the previous decades; and we should learn from our past mistake. The second is the prioritisation of mega projects. In particular, projects with high import content must be considered carefully and appropriately sequenced to limit the adverse impact on the current account. The third has to do with saving. Given that a current account deficit is the flip side of the investment-saving gap, the problem can be alleviated in part by higher domestic saving. In recent years, Thailand has relied mainly on government saving and corporate saving in financing domestic investment. Attention should focus on household saving, which now stands modestly at 4% of GDP, compared to over 10% in the 1980s. The decline in the household saving rate is attributed in part to the changing attitude of Thai consumers. As opposed to save before spend, now many people spend before they save, with the prevalence of credit cards and personal loans helping to reinforce the behaviour. Moreover, it could be a by-product of the low interest rate environment that was previously necessary to 9 facilitate the recovery of the corporate sector in the aftermath of the financial crisis. With the current upward interest rate cycle, the decline in household saving rate may be partially reversed, but this factor alone should not be enough to raise domestic saving to the desirable level. Therefore, other saving mobilization schemes deserve policy attention going forward. To sum up, Thailands growth performance is likely to be satisfactory given our economys resilience and driving factors like private investment, public investment, and exports. While world oil prices are likely to stay high for another 3-4 years and at the same time our industrial sector is seeing greater need to expand production capacity and the government is embarking on mega projects to upgrade the countrys infrastructure, the key challenge for Thailand is maintaining economic stability, especially relieving pressure off the current account. As said, we should aim at securing long-term financing for our private and public investment plans. The best solution is to raise financing from within the country in the form of higher domestic saving. However, that will take time, so we have to also maintain quality financing from abroad, especially foreign direct investment, by keeping ourselves attractive in the eyes of foreign investors. In order to do so, we need to maintain inflation within the target, keep on strengthening our banking system, and safeguard fiscal discipline. And this is the current agenda of the Bank of Thailand. 10 Ladies and gentlemen, Given the active role of the British Chamber of Commerce Thailand in promoting cordial relationship between British and Thai business communities, I hope you all will be with me on this endeavour. Thank you.

Title: Investing in Emerging Markets : A Central Bank View
text: Investing in Emerging Markets: A Central Bank View * Bandid Nijathaworn Bank of Thailand First, let me thank the organizer, HSBC Investment, for the invitation. Before we begin our panel discussion on investing in emerging markets, I want to use this opening remark to comment on two issues. First, I want to highlight some of the key changes that have brought emerging markets to where they are today. And second, I want to share with you my views on the challenges from the perspective of policy in ensuring that this renewed interest in emerging markets as an asset class does not lead to risks in terms of financial distress or economic disruptions as was the case of the past, but to a more durable and sustainable investment that brings lasting benefits to emerging markets. The growing importance of emerging market economies in the world economy, as well as improved fundamentals, have been * A remark given at Emerging Markets Conference: The Changing Nature of Emerging Market, Organized by HSBC at the Park Hyatt Hotel, Zurich, May 6th 2008. 2 highlighted by a number of speakers in the earlier sessions of this conference. But one important point that we must take note is that, as a group, the improvements in economic fundamentals and resilience in emerging markets is quite remarkable, especially considering that they were the economies that were hit by a series of financial crises less than ten years ago. Such strength clearly indicates that important changes have taken place in emerging markets, and as a group, they have made a successful recovery from those difficult years. On this issue, two observations can be made. The first is that recovery made by emerging markets is by no means a cyclical phenomenon, but a product of a careful process of restructuring and reform that has taken place. This process of reform includes improvements in the macroeconomic policy framework and institutions, centering on stability-focused monetary policy, disciplined fiscal policy, greater flexibility in the exchange rate system, and more liberal policy on capital flows. All these have worked to lower the volatilities in output and prices, strengthen the balance of payments and external positions, and regain the confidence of investors and markets. Another common element of reform is the consolidation and the strengthening of the banking sector that have led to better risk 3 management and disclosure by banks, and a more thorough approach to bank regulation based on risk-based supervision and adherence to international standards. Market opening and liberalization of the domestic economy is another common reform element that have led to a more competitive business environment in emerging markets that helped spur the growth of new companies. And last but not least is the self-insurance, in the forms of reserve accumulation and closer cooperation among emerging markets in policy and market surveillance aimed at reducing susceptibility to external shocks. This process of reform, in my view, is the really important change in the nature of emerging markets that have transformed emerging markets, as a group, to what we are seeing today. Another observation I want to make is the benefits from change that we are now seeing in emerging markets, both at the macro and the micro levels. At the macro level, we are familiar with data that point to high GDP growth rates, high savings rates, large current account surpluses, and strong balance of payment positions and international reserves. But what is more impressive is the evidence of change and dynamism at the micro level, of which three developments stand out. The first is the strength of companies in emerging markets. 4 Companies in emerging markets are making an impact at the global level and some are on their way to become new global multinationals. In 2006, the Boston Consulting Group listed one hundred of these companies in countries like China, India, Brazil, Mexico, Russia, Turkey, Malaysia and Thailand. The second is the positive attitude and belief of the new generation of the working population in emerging markets who are more confident now about their abilities and the future. This, in my view, is the most important foundation for future growth. And the third is the growth of intra-regional trade and investment driven by the dynamism of the private sector. All these are key dynamism that will help sustain the current process of change and growth in emerging markets well into the future. The second issue I want to bring up in this opening remark is the challenge for policy. In view of the ongoing uncertainty in the global economy, interest in emerging markets as an asset class has increased. In the short-term, emerging markets are seen as being better positioned to weather the externally-induced volatility. In the longer-term, outlook for continued growth in emerging markets driven by strong fundamentals and supportive demographic structure is a prospect that is widely shared in financial markets. Such outlook offers many good 5 investment themes that can accommodate a wide range of investors. These themes include infrastructure financing, development of new enterprises and companies, and the growth of intra-regional trade. As an asset class, at this time, emerging markets offer a compelling investment opportunity in terms of diversification, yield enhancement, favourable valuations, with growing set of investment and risk-management products ranging from fixed income to sovereign, equity, credit and structured products, financial derivatives and distressed assets. This range of products is a big departure from the market situation of ten years ago, and on account of this, investment opportunity in emerging markets is now being looked at by a wider set of investors, including sovereign wealth funds. Emerging markets, in general, welcome this opportunity. The increased flows of capital will allow emerging economies to tackle the remaining issues and raise long-term growth potentials. The key challenge, instead, is to ensure that these flows of capital are put into best use that will benefit emerging markets in the long-term, while any risk to stability in terms of financial distress from such flows is kept to a minimum. 6 On this, one of the key differences between emerging markets and developed economies is the extent to which macroeconomic shocks, when propagated through the economy, give rise to higher output and consumption volatility in emerging markets than in developed economies. A good example is the capital flow shocks. For example, rapid movements of capital flows into and out of Asia in the period leading up to 1997 and immediately thereafter, when interacted with financial system underdevelopment, led to a boom-bust cycle with significant costs to both short-run and long-run output growth. But for developed economies, the experience is more of the case where large shocks typically result in substantial asset price volatility and substantial financial losses that are not accompanied by major disruptions to economic growth. And a substantial part of these observed differences is attributable to the disparate level of financial sector development in these two groups of countries. This conclusion, I think, is powerful and is key for emerging markets in managing an efficient allocation of capital, as well as in managing risks to financial stability. For many emerging markets in Asia including Thailand, although the strengthening of macroeconomic stability and the banking sector has been achieved, a lot remains to be done in financial sector development so as to improve the ability of the 7 economy to absorb shocks by itself in a way that minimizes the impact on the real economy and avoids risk to financial stability. In this context, an important focus of further reform in emerging markets must be on enhancing the risk management ability of economic agents via strengthening the efficiency and the robustness of the financial system. This includes developing a well-balanced financial structure, especially the bond market, so that fixed-rate, longterm security in local currency can be offered to avoid mismatch which was a major problem of the past crisis. Development of good financial infrastructure is another important agenda in the areas of credit and pricing information, supportive legal structure, human resource development, risk-transfer mechanism, and a good system of data disclosure and accounting standards. These changes will further strengthen the financial sector, and make it more likely that the process towards greater global financial integration will bring substantial benefits to emerging markets in terms of higher growth and fewer risks, so that in the long-term, financial stability becomes more embedded in the underlying economic structure of emerging markets, as is the case of developed economies. Thank you.

text: Summary of special talk on "The Role of Thai Financial Institutions in the Future" by Mr.W.Prisiyathon Devakul Governor of the Bank of Thailand At the multipurpose building Bank of Thailand Northern Office The Governor led the speech. The BOT has proposed a plan to reshape the institution's role. The future of Thai finance has already gone to the Ministry of Finance, which the Minister of Finance has not yet dropped.
