Title: Special Talks Webinars Titled "From Rapid Relief to a Sustainable Recovery: Reflecting on a Year of Responses to COVID-19 by Central Banks and Financial Supervisors"
text: Keynote Speech From Rapid Relief to a Sustainable Recovery: Reflecting on a Year of Responses to COVID-19 by Central Banks and Financial Supervisors, organized by Third Generation Environmentalism Ltd (E3G), the Centre for Sustainable Finance at SOAS University of London, The South East Asian Central Banks (SEACEN) Research and Training Centre, and the Bennett Institute for Public Policy. Mr. Ronadol Numnonda, Deputy Governor of Financial Institutions Stability, Bank of Thailand 2 July 2021, 13.00  14.30 BST (19.00  20.30 BKK time) Good afternoon and good evening to all the participants in both the UK and the Southeast Asia time zones. With this common way of greetings nowadays it reminds us of how the COVID-19 has shaken the way we live. Not only has it shaken the way we live, it has also shaken financial stability around the globe and underscored the uncertainties and complexities of our economy. I believe the topic of the virtual event today stands at the heart of us central banks and supervisors. I would like to thank the organizers of this virtual event led by the research partnership of E3G, the Centre for Sustainable Finance at SOAS University of London, The South East Asian Central Banks (SEACEN) Research and Training Centre, and the Bennett Institute for Public Policy--a project funded by the International Network for Sustainable Financial Policy Insights, Research & Exchange (INSPIRE). Thank you for having me here today to share with you some reflections from the point of view of central bank. Distinguished guests, as much as we are firefighting these devastating impact of COVID-19, we have to look ahead to build back and take this opportunity to engrain the seeds of resiliency into our economy. Sustainable recovery is really not an option, and it is our job to design how to achieve this goal. In that regards, today, I will first reflect on some of the thinking behind our responses to COVID-19 over the past year and then share with you on how we are preparing for the future. Rapid COVID-19 relief measures In the case of Thailand, and similar to other countries, we have been hard-hit by the COVID-19 outbreak, especially the SMEs which are the backbone of our Thai economy. Last year, when the situation was still uncertain, the Ministry of Finance and the Bank of Thailand (BOT), had issued a package of measures to support liquidity to SMEs and corporates. Please allow me to briefly touch on some of these measures. 1. On SMEs, the Bank of Thailand issued two measures to preempt the worsening of the impacts as business came to a halt, especially SMEs with limited access to liquidity. First, on debt relief, we issued a Loan Payment Holiday of 6 months for SMEs. They would automatically be eligible to pause payments to the banks for 6 months, and not be considered as a missed payment. Second, on liquidity support, we provided Soft Loans of 500 billion baht at 0.01% interest to the financial institutions for 2 years. These funds would subsequently be lent to SMEs at a rate of just 2% per annum. 2. On Corporate, we established the 400 billion baht Corporate Bond Stabilization Fund to provide liquidity to firms. That has helped to prevent the panic sell-off of corporate bonds during the time. This year, even though we have seen early signs of recovery in some sectors but this recovery is likely to be uneven. The prolonged uncertainties, especially with the resurgence of COVID-19 cases in the second quarter, some businesses find it hard to continue their businesses, let alone getting additional loan or restructure their debts. Under such circumstances, we have launched two more measures to ensure distribution of liquidity to the affected groups in a targeted manner, reduce debt burden, and support the economic transformation in the period ahead. The measures include: 1. Loan facility for businesses to support viable SMEs. This is the expansion of the pool of eligible borrowers as well as expanding credit limit and loan tenor, and amending the interest rates to better support business recovery. 2. Debt restructuring through Asset Warehousing with buy-back options which allows businesses to suspend debt repayment and transfer property assets, as loan collateral, to their creditors temporarily. Such scheme would shield businesses from having to fire sell collaterals and provide opportunity to continue their businesses through the recovery. The BOT will support the program by providing low-cost funding at 0.01% per annum to financial institutions. These measures help to provide support for firms that are experiencing excessively high debt burdens but are still viable over the long term. They are, also, of a longer time horizon to ensure continued economic recovery as the pandemic has a much longer impact than we had first thought. Sustainable recovery Distinguished guests, those are rapid measures to help our economy endure a rough wave of the pandemic. The much awaited vaccines roll out has been key to fighting the COVID-19 pandemic itself as well as the economic crisis. I would like to stress here that, in the same way that vaccinations are key to alleviating the impact of the pandemic, it is of equal importance that we should also develop the vaccine of resilience to build immunity against the uncertainties of the world and towards a sustainable recovery. In a nutshell, I personally believe that this simply means building a better today that will bring out the best of the future, for our next generations. And in that regards, I will touch on two points that we at the Bank of Thailand have been focusing on: an inclusive and green recovery. First, on building back an inclusive recovery by leveraging on technology, especially focusing on SMEs who are the backbone of our economy. While we have worked hard to provide rapid relief to SMEs, we have also focused on embedding adaptability and agility into their businesses upon their recovery. Our key enabler is digital technology for SMEs which could open up their possibilities and opportunities. Our work for the past years in building digital finance infrastructure has served us well during this difficult time. The innovative real-time retail fund transfer infrastructure, called PromptPay, has enabled users to send and receive fund with free of charge through mobile banking and other means. Also, standardized or interoperable QR Code for payments, known as Thai QR Payment, has built on PromptPay infrastructure that allows customers and merchants to make payments for goods and services by scanning the QR Codes without carrying cash or money. This enables firms to continue their businesses especially when e-commerce platforms become mainstream. So far, there have been around 57 million PromptPay account registration, which is huge, given our population of around 65 million. With PromptPay and QR Code as a foundation, mobile banking accounts rose to more than 70 million accounts in March this year. Going forward, we are extending our digital infrastructures to help improve efficiency and inclusion of the Thai financial system, and even more for Micro SMEs. We are building our ecosystem that can better use data to benefit the customers. We have promoted lending that is based on alternative data so it could serve people who do not have access to credit using traditional data. Another project that we are currently driving is building a digital factoring ecosystem which aims to allow for SMEs to use their invoice to digitally apply for loans and get access to liquidity more quickly. Technology is a powerful tool and a crucial key to building back an inclusive recovery. Now, turning to my second point. Embracing green recovery. For a country vulnerable to climate change, such as Thailand, we have been affected by a number of climate-related incidents, which have resulted in massive financial losses and thus threatening the stability of the financial system. As such, ensuring that the Thai economy is resilient to climate-related risks and continues to have sustainable growth is now considered a significant role for the BOT. One may wonder if climate change policy is the mandate of a central bank. I would have to say that, as a central bank, we have to ensure the stability of the economy and that is where climate-change policy has come to play. In that regards, financial sector has a key role in building this resiliency. First, financial institutions themselves need to be resilient, and to achieve that they have to assess and manage these climate-related risks, mitigating the impacts on their lending portfolios. Second, since financial sector plays a crucial role in resource allocation, they could be key in mobilizing funds to sectors which are conducive to green recovery. Therefore, these have been our two overarching objectives: (1) mitigation of climate-related risks on financial system and (2) promotion of sustainable financial products and services. In doing so, we have actively encouraged the financial institutions to conduct business responsibly, internalizing the environmental, social, and governance (ESG) considerations. BOT recognizes that financial institutions are at varying stages of climate-related developments. So we have started off as a facilitator, opting for an industryled approach to allow for flexibilities towards standardization. We have focused on increasing awareness in the financial sector. We have also collaborated closely with other financial regulators to set (aligned) policy directions. As the momentum kicks in, we are now taking the role of an accelerator, creating a conducive ecosystem for financial institutions to comprehensively internalize climate-change risks into their decision-making. The keys to that are the development of standards and data availability to assess climaterelated opportunities and risks. So we are currently developing standardized tools and templates such as financial disclosure, taxonomy, and climate scenario analysis & stress testing that can be used across the industry. Standardization is not only crucial at the national level, but also at the regional and international level, given the significant amount of cross-border trade and financial flows as well as the interconnected supply chains. We have joined hands with our ASEAN community to create the ASEAN Taxonomy to serve as an overarching guide and a common language for the ASEAN economies. This is to ensure alignment of standards across the regions, making it easier and more practical for both investors and businesses as well as financial institutions to adopt sustainable finance. Now, while hard rule-setting is currently not our priorities, going forward as the financial industry becomes more ready and better equipped, I believe we could step more into that territory of designing regulatory and supervisory framework. These are some key areas of our work for building sustainability in financial sector, focusing on both the stability side as well as on the development side of the financial system. Conclusion Distinguished guests, we acknowledge that the road ahead is not easy. Peoples awareness in the sustainability issues, especially during the pandemic, capacity development to handle new areas of sustainability knowledge, and broader cooperation among key stakeholders, be it the financial sector, businesses, policy maker as well as academia are keys to a successful path to sustainable recovery. In this regards, we truly appreciate the work by INSPIRE as a research network to support us central banks and supervisors in managing a transition to a sustainable recovery. Todays event serves as one important initiative, bringing people together from both the public and private sectors to exchange views and plan for a better future. I truly wish you all a fruitful discussion at this virtual event today. Thank you very much for your kind attention.

Title: : SEACEN  ASEAN Core Curriculum on Climate Risk Resilience/Sustainable Finance Block 4:Regulation and Supervision
text: Welcome remarks ASEAN Core Curriculum on Climate Risk Resilience/Sustainable Finance Block 4: Regulation and Supervision Hosted by Bank of Thailand 13 February 2023, 09:00 - 09:30 Bangkok Time Dr. Mangal Goswami, Executive Director, The SEACEN Centre Professor Ulrich Volz, Professor of Economics & Director of the Centre for Sustainable Finance, SOAS, University of London Distinguished speakers, and participants Ladies and gentlemen First of all, I would like to extend a warm welcome to all participants to the ASEAN Core Curriculum on Climate Risk Resilience and Sustainable Finance Block 4: Regulation and Supervision. It is a pleasant opportunity to finally meet you in person as I believe this is the first hybrid SEACEN seminar here since 2020. On behalf of the Bank of Thailand, I would like to thank the SEACEN centre and the SOAS centre for Sustainable Finance for arranging the capacity building course on this important and urgent topic in Thailand. Ladies and Gentlemen, I am confident that all of us have already acknowledged substantial threat of climate change posing to society and economy. Central banks and financial regulators in our region and around the world have put much effort in setting a concrete policy direction towards tackling climate change. Likewise, the BOT published a directional paper on Transitioning towards Environmental Sustainability Under the New Thai Financial Landscape last year to communicate and kick start the journey with our stakeholders. It is essential for the financial sector to manage climate-related risks, while at the same time, support the economic transition. This means financial institutions have to internalize climate considerations into their business operations and risk management framework and offer financial products and services to help business transition especially in the high-emission 2 and vulnerable sectors without disrupting the economy and leaving someone behind. However, there is no denying that financial sector has substantial gaps and challenges to overcome in order to achieve such goals, particularly on the risk management perspective. Financial sector resilience would be undermined by the climate-related risks without appropriate measures in a timely manner. Thus, central banks and financial regulators have a crucial role in building capacity and facilitating guidelines and tools needed for climate-related and environmental risks. The first step should be providing concrete expectation and guidance for financial industry to uplift their business operations, risk management, and disclosure that align with international standards. Simultaneously, the infrastructures and common tools for climate risk management such as climate scenario analysis, stress test, and climate-related data must be put in place to create an enabling ecosystem where financial institutions and regulators could assess and monitor the risks effectively. Ladies and Gentlemen, Looking ahead, it is thus inevitable that our regulatory and supervisory frameworks should take into account sustainability and climate-related factors. The conduct of prudential framework in this new landscape will arguably be the most difficult task as it is relatively new and still evolving. In addition, developing economies also have the distinct contexts and challenges to consider, especially on the expertise, data availability, and collaboration between public and private sector. Hence, this course is essential for us SEACEN regulators to understand and identify our gaps, learn the key rationale why such frameworks and tools are being recommended and, more importantly, the implementation of cutting-edge practices that have been tested and adopted internationally. We are greatly fortunate to have such a prominent list of experts to share their insights and experiences on these topics. 3 I would like to end my remarks by emphasizing the importance of regulators capacity and collaboration. Tackling sustainable finance and climate change is a challenging process and a long journey that cannot be accomplished by solely single entity. Not only do financial institutions, but central banks and financial regulators also need to learn, share, and accommodate these new approaches to ensure sufficient measures and readiness of the whole financial sector for climate risk management and green transition. I hope you all have a good learning experience and a successful course. Thank you very much.

Title: Sustainability Forum 2024  Financial Dynamic for Sustainability
text: Sustainability Forum 2024  Financial Dynamic for Sustainability    Deputy Governor for Financial Institution StabilityThursday , December 14, 2023 9.30 a.m. - 9.50 a.m. at Grand Hall Baithet, Bangna. Hello. Executives, Bangkok Business and Nation Group Speakers, distinguished guests, and all the media.  First of all, I would like to thank Bangkok Business for inviting me to participate in the Sustainability Forum 2024 and am honored to give a special speech on the topic of Financial Dynamics for Sustainability to highlight the role and importance of the financial sector in driving the country towards sustainability.  Today, I think everyone is aware of the importance and necessity of Operating a business that takes into account the dimensions of sustainability, especially environmental and environmental sustainability. Climate change caused by natural disasters and their direction. Greenhouse gas emission reduction policies at the global stage from the 28th UN Climate Change conferences or COP28 in Dubai, United Arab Emirates, in the past two weeks. Nearly 200 member countries have agreed to establish a Loss and Damage Fund to help vulnerable countries. Facing the worst impacts of climate change However, the first and most important thing is that we must understand the context of the Thailand in the dimension of climate change and the environment first. We are seeing climate change, accelerating through disasters, becoming more severe, hotter, and longer. The cold is shortened, and the flood is severe. The Thai economy is vulnerable to natural disasters (physical risk), ranking 1 in 10 in the world. Especially in the agriculture and tourism sectors, but with the capacity to cope with climate change, it ranks last (39 out of 48 countries). Most of Thailand's industrial sectors are still in the brown group, which is a risk that we call transition risk, that is, they still rely on a high proportion of coal and oil energy and/or still use old technologies that emit gas. Greenhouses at a high level, which will face pressure to adapt. o Awareness and readiness in environmental dimensions that lead to Although large businesses have begun to adapt, Thai companies have become members of the DJSI (Dow Jones Sustainability Index), the highest in ASEAN countries, and 12 companies are in the gold class, the most in the world. It is fragile and has less awareness and readiness than large businesses. o Thailand also faces other environmental problems such as the problem of PM 2.5 pollution that is much more severe, especially at the end of the year to the beginning of the year, which is the tourist season in Thailand. For the reasons I mentioned above. Therefore, the Thai economic sector and financial institutions need to adapt both to transition to environmental sustainability in terms of reducing greenhouse gas emissions and pollution (mitigation) and adapting to cope with the impacts of climate change and other environmental impacts (adaptation). at the same time The government has realized the urgent need. In driving Concrete climate change goals By Declared a clear intention since COP26 to achieve the goal of neutrality. Carbon by 2050 and set a target of net zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2065 to encourage the country to drive this project. In order to lead the country to grow by taking into account the environmental dimension and climate change. The financial sector must play an important role. In providing financial support to drive the economic sector to be able to adjust in a timely manner. However, this is a new issue for the financial sector and there are still uncertainties in many aspects, making support or capital allocation not yet fully and on point. An important principle in adapting in the context of Thailand is to take into account the timing and speed that are appropriate to the context of the country, which must create a balance between moving towards the goals of sustainability and prevention. The negative side effects that will occur to various sectors by taking action must be "not too fast" so that the impact cannot be corrected, and "not too fast" so that the economic system cannot adapt quickly and leave no one behind. In order to make the adaptation appropriate. The financial institution sector must be able to assess environmental factors, both risk and opportunity, and integrate them into the business process. Bank of Thailand (BOT) has collaborated with many sectors to develop important infrastructure, helping to upgrade Consideration of environmental factors of financial institutions in 2 matters Subject T, 1 is the establishment of good practices or operational standards that take into account the environment of financial institutions (Standard Practice). Policy Guidelines on Financial Institution Business Operations Taking into account the Environment and Climate Change on February 15 in order for financial institutions to integrate environmental factors. In the process of business operations, from 1) Determining the responsibility structure for directors and senior executives. 2) Formulation of strategies taking into account environmental risks and opportunities, 3) Environmental risk management from upstream to downstream, as well as 4) Disclosure of information in accordance with international standards. In addition, the Thai Bankers Association has developed an Industry Handbook to help commercial banks refer to the Examples of international guidelines recommended and implemented, as well as identifying important processes that financial institutions should implement quickly. The second issue is the preparation of a standard for grouping economic activities or Taxonomy, which is a tool for determining the definition of greenness of all sectors to be agreed upon and agreed upon to reduce the problem of greenwashing. In order to push for a central standard that is suitable for the Thai context and in line with international principles, the Thailand Taxonomy Phase 1 covering the energy sector and the public sector has been published on June 30, 2023. The yellow group is in line with Thailand's net-zero greenhouse gas emission target for Taxonomy in the next phase. The BOT will collaborate with relevant agencies for development in other important economic sectors, including the industrial sector. Manufacturing, agriculture and construction sectors Honorable Sir, the plan that the BOT is currently focusing on is to help financial institutions in Thailand support the Thai business sector to be able to adjust their financial needs. During the transition period, it is practically effective. The BOT has determined The expectation is that commercial banks, especially large banks, will begin to formulate plans and targets to help the business sector adapt to see concrete results. By focusing on industry groups that are significant to the Environment and Climate Change, which is expected to have two results in 2024. o Result 1 is that financial institutions have products and services that meet the requirements. Transition finance product - What is the definition of a Transition Finance Product? In the international world, it usually refers to financial products which help support businesses to invest in the transition to gas reduction. Corporate greenhouses with indicators and clear tracking, such as sustainability-linked loans or It is expected that financial institutions will issue products to support the business sector to make tangible adjustments, starting with industries with high greenhouse gas emissions. The second outcome is that financial institutions have begun to have a clearer and practical transition plan.  The Transition Plan is an important mechanism for the business and financial sectors. Although there are still various definitions today, it usually refers to a business sector's plan that specifies a goal. The company has a plan to adjust its own business to achieve its goals. Reducing greenhouse gases  For the financial sector, the establishment of the institution's transition plan. International finance mostly refers to gas reduction plans. The BOT is working with commercial banks, especially large banks, to develop a transition plan for at least one of their own priority sectors by the end of 2024.  However, the formulation of the Transition Plan is still new for financial institutions in Thailand. There are guidelines and resources available for reference. In order to continue to develop their own transition plan. Distinguished Ladies and Gentlemen, you may have a question about the direction of the adjustment of both the financial sector and the real economy. O For information issues Having quality and reliable information will help. This will build confidence among investors and consumers and reduce reputational risks that may be caused by greenwashing. Finance in Thailand is still difficult due to the fragmentation and high cost of data collection, which is a major challenge in the development of transition plans and products. O What I want to emphasize is that we don't have to wait for accurate information. Before the herpes operation, financial institutions can communicate with customers to issue products to support customer groups who want to adapt clearly, which will be an example case to help create momentum that can expand the impact in a real way. O At the same time, it must be acknowledged that the financial sector cannot follow this journey on its own, even though financial institutions have environmental information according to international standards or can develop transition plans and products, but they may not be able to adapt. If there is no demand from the business sector to walk together. Therefore, the business sector should cooperate closely with financial institutions to transmit quality and reliable information on environmental business operations, as well as help SMEs in the supply chain to be ready to adapt, which will enable financial institutions to help customers plan their adaptation and offer products and services that support the adaptation of the business sector appropriately.  Lastly, the plans and targets of the BOT and the financial institution sector mentioned above are only part of the support for the goal of implementing a friendly environment for the country. however Pushing and developing the country to grow sustainably in the environment. In the coming period, it is necessary to provide The importance of other dimensions along with each other, especially the adaptation dimension. In response to the impacts of climate change and other environmental impacts, such as the mobilization of the Loss and Damage Fund to deal with the loss and damage that occurred, from the recent COP28 meeting, it can be seen that this issue is an issue that is of global importance. In the next phase, the country's framework and targets on adaptation will be the direction and action plan in this regard, and how the financial sector will play a role in supporting it. Thank you.

Title: Opening Remarks of Thailand  Japan Joint Trade and Economic Committee on 'Global Economic Conditions and Thai Economic Outlook'
text: Opening Remarks Thailand - Japan Joint Trade and Economic Committee Between the Joint Committee of the Private Sector of 3 Institutions (KOR) and Keidanren (Japan Business Federation) The topic "Global Economic Conditions and Thai Economic Trends" by Mr. Methi Supapong Deputy Governor of the Ministry of Finance, Thursday, March 16 , 2023, 09.00 a.m. - 10.00 a.m. at Royal Orchid Sheraton Hotel (Ballroom) learn Chairman of the Joint Committee of the Private Sector of 3 Institutions Chairman of the Japan Business Federation (Kedanren) Ambassador of Japan to Thailand Distinguished persons and all the media. I am very pleased to be one of the opening speakers today. I would like to thank the Japan Business Federation (Kedanren) and the Joint Committee of the Three Private Sector Institutions (KOR) for playing an important role in promoting good cooperation between Japan and Thailand in the fields of economy, trade, industry and investment. Since more than 40 years ago, the Thai government has launched the Eastern Seaboard (ESB) development project. This is reflected in the nearly 300 projects that Japanese investors have applied for investment promotion (BOI) with an investment value of about 50 billion baht, which are in many industries such as electronics and electrical appliances, chemicals and paper, as well as machinery and metals. I sincerely hope that the relationship between the two countries will continue to grow sustainably. I would like to take this opportunity to discuss the global and Thai economic outlook from the perspective of the BOT so that everyone can see the picture together to lead the economy to grow and develop in the next step. Honorable Sir, As you all know, the world economy is highly linked to the Thai economy and finance. After the COVID-19 crisis situation eased. There are still various factors that avoid pressure on the global economy. Russia-Ukraine conflict The tense relationship between the United States and China, as well as the volatile global financial markets, due to the direction of interest rate hikes. and most recently, from the problems of some financial institutions in the United States. Some financial institutions in Europe are currently in trouble. This year, the International Monetary Fund estimates that the global economy will slow down from last year, but the latest data at the beginning of the year suggests that the chances of a severe contraction in the global economy are less likely to be in line with the economic outlook of major countries, including China. The United States The labor market is still strong.) However, the impact of interest rate hikes must be monitored. Policies on the economy, including the impact on the financial system, such as the T Crisis, occurred with some banks. In the United States Meanwhile, the Euro Economic figures for the fourth quarter of last year came out better than expected in many countries, which is considered that Europe has gone through a thousand energy crises during the winter well. As part of this, fears of a recession in Europe have eased as well. As a result, the economy is expected to continue to expand slightly positively this year. For China The faster than expected reopening of the country and the Chinese authorities' signal to take more measures to support economic growth and maintain stability in the real estate sector have made Domestic demand is expected to improve in line with pent-up demand and higher savings of Chinese households. After a long lockdown, it will encourage China's economy to grow faster this year to about 5% from only 3% last year. In addition, it will also result in The economies of other countries, especially in Asia, expanded better along with China's economy. The development of global inflation is still unreliable. Although the prices of energy products, especially fuel oil and gas, have decreased, it is expected that the gradual decline in inflation in major economies such as the United States, the euro area, and the United Kingdom will remain higher. The target framework will continue until next year, making it expected that interest rates will increase. It reached its peak and remained at a high level for a while. In addition, there is another major risk that will squeeze the global economy. The global financial market fluctuated due to interest rate hikes, which were relatively fast and strong in many major countries. This has resulted in higher financial conditions and fundraising costs. This has continuously caused fluctuations in capital flows and currencies, as well as affecting the liquidity of some financial institutions. In the US, there is a sequin in the value of assets. Undermining the confidence of depositors until it has to be terminated by the authorities. Finally Operation however Thailand's financial and economic system has good foreign stability, including our foreign debt at the eye level, including companies with a high proportion of short-term foreign debt, which is less than 25%. Therefore, this foreign strength has helped Thailand cope with the impact of external factors in the past. In terms of the Thai economy, it is expected that the Thai economy will continue to recover. The economy is expected to expand by about 3.7 percent this year, higher than last year's 2.6 percent expansion. There is a good and continuous trend of recovery. Especially when China opened the country earlier than expected. The BOT expects the total number of foreign tourists this year to be around 25.5 million, higher than last year's 11.1 million (the number of Chinese tourists is forecast to be 5 million), while next year it is expected that there will be a total of about 34 million foreign tourists. However, at the end of this month, The BOT will issue a New Economic Estimates Therefore, the number may be different from what is said today. The recovery of the tourism sector will also support economic activities in other service sectors and is an important factor contributing to private consumption. Service sector activities that are resilient This will have a positive impact on employment and income distribution of many employees and self-employed people, which will help increase the purchasing power of households and multiply the result. (multiplier effect) on private sector consumption. Although Thailand's exports may expand more or not at all due to the impact of the slowdown in global trade, exports are expected to expand better next year in line with the recovery of the global economy and trade. As the economy recovers, private investment is likely to return more in the coming period, as reflected by the value of the BOI issued which has expanded significantly in the post-COVID period. including investment in digital technology infrastructure such as Cloud Storage & Data center, which will return investment, especially in the new global industry, will be a key driver of the economy in the next phase. For Thailand, headline inflation is likely to continue to decline. Supply-side inflationary pressures are gradually easing as global energy and commodity prices decline and are expected to return to the target range of 1-3% in the next quarter of this year. However, it is important to monitor the risk that core inflation (headline inflation minus the price of fresh food and energy products) may remain at a higher level for longer than in the past. This is due to the fact that entrepreneurs are facing high costs and some types of cost prices are still at a high level, such as domestic energy prices that may fall below global energy prices. From the gradual collection of money into the oil fund, which is currently still negative, as well as inflationary pressure on the demand side that may increase due to the rapid recovery of the tourism sector. Next, I would like to discuss the direction of Thailand's monetary policy that must be considered in parallel with economic recovery, price stability, and financial system stability. At the same time, the easing of monetary policy by gradually raising the policy rate while adjusting the size and timing of the policy rate hike. If the economic outlook and inflation deviate from the estimated (gradual and measured policy normalization), it is still an appropriate approach. It also facilitates the borrowing costs of the private sector. All sectors have been able to adapt and continue to implement debt restructuring measures by focusing on specific measures and sustainable debt solutions for vulnerable groups, especially SMEs and households with high debt burdens. After looking at the global economic picture and the Thai economic outlook at the same time. I would like to invite you to look back and see what are the strengths that make Thailand attractive for investors who will invest and do business together. There are 3 things in total. The first is Thailand. It is the second largest economy in the ASEAN group. which is the largest economic group in the world. In addition, ASEAN countries have quite a lot of trade links between them. This is reflected in the three-fold increase in intra-regional trade over the past two decades and the proportion of global direct investment flowing into the region, which continues to increase. During the COVID-19 pandemic, foreign direct investment in 2021 has returned to pre-COVID levels , and excluding direct investment, has entered Singapore, Asia's financial hub. 1/4 of this money is investment flowing into Thailand. Second, Thailand's infrastructure and public utilities are ready and create links in various fields such as investment, production, and labor, so Thailand has the potential to become a one-stop service center to facilitate the region through the cooperation of the public and private sectors. In setting guidelines for economic development to support the world. future In terms of transportation, Thailand has a good transportation system, according to the World Bank's International Logistics Performance Index, which considers transportation costs, time, transportation time, and transportation reliability. Thailand ranks second in the country with the most advanced transportation system in ASEAN, second only to Singapore, and is developing even better in the next phase. Third, now is a good time to invest and do business in Thailand. The economy is recovering steadily and the government has measures and tools to adequately maintain economic stability in both the financial and fiscal sectors. Domestic consumption is expected to go well with better incomes and investment is trending better, ensuring that Thailand will be a production base, can be linked to other markets, and is ready to become a center of production and investment in the midst of an increasingly decoupled global economy. I would like to conclude by adapting to the context of a new world. From the perspective of the business sector. Maintaining competitiveness is a major challenge, requiring resiliency and higher efficiency and productivity, which will help businesses to withstand and adapt to shocks. Meanwhile, Leveraging digital technology in finance and other areas to develop innovation will reduce both financial costs and time. Reduce errors and increase business revenue. In addition, environmental sustainability is another factor that will help increase Thailand's competitiveness, and investment in environmentally friendly industries will be in line with Thailand's goal of carbon neutrality by 2050 and the goal of environmental sustainability. The BOT has also accelerated the reduction in three areas: (1) formulating a policy line that will accelerate the implementation of greenhouse gases by 2065, and (2) establishing a policy guideline for financial institutions; (2) Supporting the transformation loan to create incentives to reduce the burden of adaptation costs, and (3) Preparing a taxonomy suitable for the Thai context. Starting with the energy and transportation sectors this year and the industrial and agricultural sectors next year. Finally, I would like to conclude that although the global economy is slowing down this year, the Thai economy is likely to recover. It has strengths both as a country and as a link in the ASEAN region. It is a good time to increase investment, especially in new industries, both in technology and environmentally friendly industries. (Strategic Partner) of Thailand. In adapting to the world under a new context, we will continue to work together. Thank you.

text: Opening Speech of the Debt Relief Expo Dr. Sethaput Sutthiwatanaruput, Governor of the Bank of Thailand Monday 26 September 2022 Session 1 Opening Ceremony at 13.20 - 13.30 hrs. Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Energy Minister of Finance Chairman of the Thai Bankers Association, the International Bankers Association and the Thai Leasing Business Association Vice Chairman of the Association of State Financial Institutions Journalists and all honorable persons. Household debt is a structural problem of the Thai economy that has been accumulating for a long time and has been exacerbated by the previous crisis. During the COVID-19 crisis, household debt remained at 60% of GDP in 2010, and household debt increased to 80% in 2019 and to 90% in the first quarter of 2021 due to COVID-19, and most recently in the second quarter of 2022 it decreased to 88%. During COVID As of July 2020 , financial institutions have assisted a maximum of 12.5 million debtors, with a total debt of 7.2 trillion baht, accounting for about 40% of the total loans, before gradually decreasing due to the economic climb . In addition, the BOT has enhanced the level of supervision of financial services in a fair manner, such as charging default interest on the basis of principal and actual default, and adjusting the order of debt cancellation to reduce the debt burden of the people and reduce the possibility of bad debts in the system. Although the Thai economy has improved due to the impact of COVID-19 and is expected to expand. However, the balance in each sector is still uneven. Especially the self-employed or low-income groups who are still facing the high cost of living, which may exacerbate the vulnerability of debtors and exacerbate the household debt problem, which may affect the economic recovery in the next period. Honorable Sir, In order for the Thai economy to continue to be resilient. Therefore, the solution to household debt must have 3 main components. One, do it in a comprehensive way. In accordance with the nature and causes of problems at each stage of debt, before incurring debts, financial discipline must be created for debtors. Meanwhile, creditors must release debts in a quality manner that is consistent with their ability to repay debts and provide sufficient information for borrowers' decisions, such as responsible lending. In order to avoid the accumulation of risk-based pricing mechanisms that will help good debtors receive reduced interest rates suitable for their risks, as well as to have a way to refinance debts more conveniently at a reasonable cost, and when there is a problem with debt repayment, there should be a mechanism to support standardized debt resolution to help debtors get out of the debt cycle in practice, such as debt mediation outside the court. Debt resolution with multiple creditors Second, do it in a principled manner by considering the appropriate approach and know what to do and what not to do (Do's and Don'ts), which are mainly (1) to solve debts on the spot, in line with the problems of debtors who do not do it on a broad scale because the financial sector will have fewer resources to help debtors who really need it, and (2) not to create additional burdens on debtors in the future, such as suspending debt repayment until the debtor has an increased interest burden. (3) Do not reduce the opportunity to access credit, such as deleting or correcting the debtor's credit history. and (4) creditors and debtors must cooperate and be sincere in resolving debts, for example, creditors must help to suit their ability to repay debts. Complete and accurate information to ensure the success of debt settlement. It takes time because Thai household debt is a long-standing problem and is caused by many reasons, both from creditors and debtors. Doing something that looks good or looks fast may not be sustainable. Third, integrate cooperation from all sectors, including the financial sector as creditors, who must provide new loans by taking into account the potential of their children to repay debts, while providing information that does not stimulate excessive debt. Government It plays a role in generating income and preparing infrastructure, especially in the field of data, which is conducive to solving problems. Sustainable household debt in the private sector Enhance the role of employers in taking care of debt problems of employees and debtors. They must strengthen their financial immunity, incur debts by taking into account their own potential, and be disciplined in repaying debts. In the past, The BOT has implemented debt resolution measures based on the above guidelines, and this Debt Resolution Expo is a continuation of what the BOT has been doing. Honorable Sir, Today, the BOT is very pleased that various sectors have recognized the importance of solving household debt problems by jointly organizing the "Debt Resolution Symposium for Debt Resolution and Sustainable Restart" to help vulnerable debtors who are facing debt repayment problems to be able to move forward. In the next phase. The BOT will issue a policy to solve the structural debt problem in a sustainable manner. (Directional Paper) by 2022 to communicate the direction. Operations, BOT In the future, the Bank will push forward and work with other sectors to help drive concrete solutions as soon as possible, such as issuing clearer responsible lending rules, which covers the issuance of new and quality debts and the provision of information that debtors should know in order to adjust their behavior to be financially disciplined and reduce excessive debt. Lastly, I would like to thank the relevant agencies, both the government and the financial sector, for working together strongly over the past time and will continue to drive the plan. To help debtors get through this crisis and make the Thai economy stable and sustainable. Thank you.

Title: Global Risks and the Outlook for Thailand Governor of the Bank of Thailand in his opening remarks at Fitch Ratings (Thailand)'s 10th Anniversary Annual Conference Conrad Hotel Bangkok
text: Global Risks and the Outlook for Thailand By Dr. Prasarn Trairatvorakul Governor, Bank of Thailand Address at the Fitch Ratings (Thailand)s 10th Anniversary Annual Conference Thursday, 1 September 2011, 09.00-09.15 at Conrad Hotel Bangkok Distinguished speakers and panelists, Ladies and Gentlemen, I would like to thank Fitch Ratings (Thailand)s for inviting me to give an opening address at this year 10th Anniversary Annual Conference. I also like to say that the conference theme Global Risks and Outlook for Thailand is most timely and should stimulate quite active discussion among the distinguished audience in this room. I am sure that the conference will help bring new insights on how we should look at the world, advanced, and Asian economies in the period ahead underlined by great uncertainties. For my part, I would like to highlight some key issues that can have potentially significant policy implications. I will touch briefly on three areas, namely the prospects of the advanced and Asian economies, Thailands economic outlook, and finally the key policy challenges going forward. At the outset, it is fair to say that prospects of the global economy could be quite murky over the year ahead. There are greater uncertainties with regard to the speed of recovery and additional policy actions in the US and Eurozone economies, and the risks of misforecasting are high. Worldwide, policymakers and markets have anticipated that the US sluggish recovery could face further downside risks as US fiscal and monetary policies could run out of bullets to provide the much needed stimulus. For the Eurozone, doubts on the potential contagion of sovereign debt crisis to other European countries remain, reflecting the ineffective impact of domestic policy on the economic recovery in these economies. Looking ahead, a more positive sentiment on the Eurozone is contingent on the growth performance of Germany and France in particular. But, recent signs of economic weakness in external and domestic demand in these countries have been somewhat worrisome, and new data release could either calm or jerk market sentiments. Despite these rather gloomy prospects in advanced economies, I remain cautiously optimistic on the performance of Asian economies for the rest of this 2 year. My assessment is conditional on the ability of Asian economies to maintain economic resilience and pursue an appropriate policy mix to preserve economic and financial stability. Evidenced since the 2009 US crisis, major economies in Asia have been able to cushion the adverse impact of global economic roller coaster by expanding domestic demand, supported by expansionary fiscal policy and monetary accommodation. Once world trade has resumed growth after the initial contraction in the aftermath of 2008 US crisis, Asian exports have continued to grow robustly on the back of regional trade expansion and strong growth in Asia, particularly China and India. Notably, some studies have shown that the ratio of Asian exports for final consumption within Asia has risen, though varying among individual countries. For example, approximately 70 percent of Indonesian exports to China are for final consumption in China. Such ratios for Singapore and Korea are 50 and 40 percent, respectively. That said, it is wise not to jump quickly to conclusion because Asian economies and trade remain critically linked to the G3 economies. While this negative spillover from advanced economies to Asian economies could be partially cushioned on the trade side, I have greater concern on the potential spillover through volatility in international capital flow and financial market movements. In addition to the risk aversion in time of market stress, emerging market economies have tried to live with spillover from exceptionally easy monetary policy in advanced countries. Such practices have created excess global liquidity leading to volatile capital flows into emerging market countries including Thailand. Moreover, excess global liquidity has been an important factor behind the rapid rise in oil and other commodity prices. Unless the advanced economies manage to get themselves out of sluggish growth path, all of us have to be vigilant and cannot rule out the possibility that the US may need to find creative policy actions to stimulate its economy. And the impact of these efforts on emerging markets can be quite unpredictable and inconsistent with economic theories, due to the international currency status of the US dollar and the safe haven status of US dollar investment. Distinguished audience, Against the background of quite an unpredictable external environment, I believe that the Thai economy would still turn in reasonable growth rate for the year 2011. On the demand side, I see consumption and investment continuing on the rise. Consumer spending is expected to benefit from a high level of farm income from rising output and agricultural prices, high employment, and good 3 consumer confidence. Meanwhile, investment by the private sector is also expected to grow, though at a slower rate than the periods following the crisis recovery. Currently, business sentiment and future investment plans are still showing an improving sign. And, public investment spending remains a key factor to keep demand momentum going forward. What we need to assess more cautiously is the future export performance. Of course, our export sector would be affected by the slowdown in the global economy to the extent that a large proportion of final demand for Asian and Thai exports remains in G3 economies. Having said that, I believe that exports will continue to grow along with world trade as long as the US and EU growth slowdown does not cause another global recession. I also want to stress that the process of export diversification in Thailand has advanced continuously in terms of markets and products. Today, the proportion of Thai exports to non-G3 countries growing significantly higher, particularly to China, and ASEAN. In parallel, the share of G3 in Thai exports has declined from more than 50 percent in 1995 to less than one-third. Ladies and Gentlemen, Turning to the final part of my talk. As a central banker, our challenge is to constantly weigh the balance between risks from global slowdown on our economic growth versus rising domestic inflation pressure. Despite more downside risk on growth at present, the central bank assesses that the Thai economy is growing at around its potential and demand pressure could transmit readily to higher inflation outcome as well as expectations. To this end, the Monetary Policy Committee has been raising the policy rate to normalize monetary policy and bring the real policy rate closer to the positive range, yet remaining sufficiently accommodative to cushion the downside risk on growth. With many uncertainties ahead, it is wise to keep the inflation rate low to ensure that the economy remains competitive and to minimize pockets of instability, whether through excessive growth of bank credits, fiscal spending, or asset price bubbles. Low inflation helps keep the health of the economy in check and preserve the purchasing power or real income of all segments of the population. This is especially important for salary earners and the poor, whose real income could easily by eroded by higher inflation. Worse is to allow inflation expectation to run away because it will be costly to get expectation well anchored again. 4 Worth noting is that, similarly to Thailand, many Asian economies have also capitalized on the opportunities to lessen monetary policy easing during the period of good economic performance since the latter part of 2010. The main objective has been to preserve fiscal and monetary policy space for potentially more difficult times ahead. For Thailand, I believe that our policy space remains appropriate. But, any higher public spending should be done with special care. At this juncture, the need to increase government consumption is less urgent and the fiscal focus should be put on public investment to expand our potential output. Therefore, the stimulus should be prioritized and carefully planned to leave some policy space for future needs. Ladies and gentlemen, I would like to end my talk today by stressing that we now live in a different and difficult world. Current global risks from the slowdown in advanced economies have clearly heightened. Given good economic fundamentals, the Thai economy should be resilient enough to cope with such risks. I would like to urge investors not to swing between over pessimism and over-confidence and behave in a herd-like manner. Instead, all parties, public and private, should be cautious and prepared for the global risks in moving the country forward. It is my firm believe that protecting domestic purchasing power and let everyone have equal chance to benefit from the economic growth can strengthen the future well being of the Thai economy in a sustainable manner in years ahead. Without further delay, may I officially open the Fitch Ratings (Thailand)s 2011 10th Anniversary Annual Conference and wish everyone a fruitful deliberation. Thank you for your attention.

Title: BOT Digital Finance Conference 2023   "Building Ecosystem for Responsible Innovation"
text: BOT Digital Finance Conference 2023 "Building Ecosystem for Responsible Innovation" Keynote Address by Governor of the Bank of Thailand (14 September 2023 10.15-10.30) Introduction: Financial landscape... to digital finance development  BOT announced Financial Landscape Consultation Paper in February 2022 as key directions for repositioning the financial sector to support sustainable digital economy.  We want to see the financial sector able to leverage on technology and data to drive innovation and better financial services through Open Data, Open Infrastructure, Open Competition.  The key directions - the 3-Opencontinue to guide us to build an ecosystem for responsible innovation where different players, through a healthy competition and a balance between innovation and risks, develop financial services that better meet consumer needs. With great collaboration with the industry and other government agencies, what we have together achieved so far: 1. Open Infrastructure a. mBridge - The platform designed to support real-time, cross-border payments using CBDCs. The platform, developed by BIS Innovation Hub and 4 countries1, has successfully completed its pilot phase (with 164 transactions, worth over US22 million) and shown potential benefits : (1) faster transfer time from 3-5 days to several seconds; (2) potentially up to 40% lower funding costs (Nostro-vostro liquidity), FX costs and compliance costs; (3) reduce settlement risk with atomic PvP settlement;2 (4) mBridge also provides traceability of the transactions (which cannot be traced in the current system) b. PromptPay & PayNow - the worlds first linkage of faster payment systems. A total of 900,000 transactions worth US190 million taking place since inception in April 2021.3 c. QR code payment linkages with 6 countries. Thailand has implemented the highest number of cross-border direct real-time payment linkages in the world. d. PromptBiz - The new digital infrastructure, launched last month, aims to facilitate digital trade and payment processes for business. 2. Open Data- BOT and banking industry launched dStatement last year, the digital service facilitates customers to efficiently request and send bank statement information across banks and enables a digital lending process with lower operating costs. 3. Open Oompetition-BOT has provided the draft regulation on Virtual Bank to the Ministry of Finance in July. 1 Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), the Bank of Thailand (BoT), the Central Bank of the United Arab Emirates (CBUAE), the Digital Currency Research Institute of the People's Bank of China (PBC DCI) 2 According to BIS (2022), US 2.2 trillion of daily FX turnover was subjected to settlement risk. 3 Latest data as of May 2023. Next phase: But, we want to do more to enhance this ecosystem. There still exist frictions to access and transfer our own data which are generated with various service providers. We need to make it easier for players to access key digital infrastructure which will be less costly for players to enter the market. We must ensure that the foundational layer for innovation is there and players have room to experiment with new technology. What we still need to do more? 1. Common utility 2. Open digital payment ecosystem 3. Collaborative approach to new technology 1. Common utility - as public goods for digital finance development. We will focus on Consumer empowerment ecosystem [data] where consumers exercise their rights to transfer their data stored at one provider to another. For example, a loan applicant can reguest to transfer their bank account information, utility usage/bill payment data and other alternative data from one service provider to another so that lenders assess the applicants risk and offer better tailored products. With reduced friction on data portability, consumers can leverage the use of their own data to get better services and access to financing from different service providers.  Regulations and incentives to ensure that service providers put in place a mechanism which enables data owners to reguest and transfer their data from one service provider to another via digital channels, i.e., Data in a machine-readable format, Secure data sharing under common standards and data governance, with supportive pricing structure.  Common standards to reduce development costs and ensure secure data sharing among various types of financial/non-financial service providers. The BOT will facilitate the consultation and standard setting for common data standard, API standard, and security standard with banks, nonbanks, and standard specialists such as Electronic Transactions Development Agency (ETDA) and Digital Government Agency (DGA). First, we are focusing on efficient data sharing among service providers under BOT supervision (banks and nonbanks) with customers consent. Then, we are also hoping to extend the ecosystem to Involve both data sources and data consumers In other sectors, such as utility usage/bill payment. We look to seek collaboration with the industry to explore use cases that common infrastructures can be utilized to streamline common processes or shared services. This will allow service providers to connect to key digital infrastructure with common standards, reduce investment cost and time to market, and enhance overall system efficiency. 2. Open digital payment ecosystem - ensuring fair access to key digital payment infrastructure to support open competition among players and having an integrated strategic direction towards more digital payment and less-cash society.  Revise regulation to ensure qualified players are able to access to systemically Important retail payment systems (i.e. NITMX) and allow them to engage in setting the direction for infrastructure development.  Review payment fee structure to support players access to digital payment Infrastructure and digital payment adoption. Currently work in progress by a fee structure working group and stakeholder consultation with industry.  Formulate an Integrated strategy for driving digital payment adoption in each customer segment so that Thailand can transition more smoothly into a less-cash society. BOT will need to engage and collaborate with relevant stakeholders for effective implementation and smooth transition. At the same time, we need to take care of financial inclusion where cash still plays an important role in many areas. 3. Collaborative approach to new technology - we want to explore new use cases with the industry for the use of new technology (such as tokenization, programmability, and Al) in the financial sector under a suitable risk framework.  New Sandbox: Currently, BOT has the Regulatory Sandbox, which allows testing of regulated activities that have the application of new technologies. What we are planning to do is to have an additional channel, the New Sandbox which is more flexible, to support the testing of unregulated financial activities that apply new technologies for use cases that benefit customers (e.g. tokenization that helps improve access to credit for SMEs, programmability that helps enhance efficiency of payment services)  Al: BOT will engage with stakeholders and explore possibility to better utilize Al in financial services (e.g. fraud prevention & detection and financial inclusion) with proper risk management framework. Closing: Collaboration for building ecosystem  BOT plans to publish a consultation paper on these strategic directions by early Q4 2023 to receive feedbacks and suggestions from stakeholders.  We cannot do this alone. Building the ecosystem for responsible innovation requires collaboration, strength, and expertise of all stakeholders (banks, non-banks, end users, technology companies, regulators in both financial and non-financial sectors) to design and implement.  The BOT Digital Finance Conference today is an example that BOT can provide a platform for financial industry to collaborate, to share knowledge, expertise, and to foster innovation.  Thank you for your effective collaboration with BOT and I am looking forward to a closer partnership in the future.
